Justification: Aedes albopictus, commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito, is one of the most significant invasive vectors of human pathogens globally. It is a highly competent vector for several arboviruses, most notably Dengue (all four serotypes), Chikungunya, and Zika. Unlike Aedes aegypti, which is highly anthropophilic, Ae. albopictus is an opportunistic feeder (eclectic), biting humans, mammals, and birds, which allows it to act as a "bridge vector" for zoonotic diseases such as West Nile virus and various Encephalitis viruses. Furthermore, it is a primary vector for the filarial nematodes Dirofilaria immitis and Dirofilaria repens. Its ecological plasticity, particularly its ability to undergo diapause in the egg stage, has allowed it to colonize temperate regions, significantly expanding the geographical risk area for tropical diseases.

Anopheles albitarsis is a valid species and the nominal member of the Albitarsis Complex within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. Historically treated as a single polymorphic species, integrated taxonomic approaches—including DNA barcoding (COI), ITS2 sequencing, and morphological analysis—have revealed it to be a species complex currently comprising several distinct lineages (e.g., An. albitarsis s.s., An. deaneorum, An. marajoara, An. oryzivorus, and An. janconnae). The name remains taxonomically stable for the populations corresponding to the original description by Lynch Arribálzaga in Argentina.

Anopheles noroesteensis Galvão & Lane, 1937 is currently treated as a junior synonym of Anopheles (Nyssorhynchus) evansae (Brèthes, 1926). The species was originally described based on morphological characters of the eggs and male genitalia from specimens collected in São Paulo, Brazil. However, subsequent taxonomic revisions, most notably by Lane (1953), established the synonymy after comparing the type material and recognizing that the morphological variations fell within the range of An. evansae. This classification is maintained in the current mosquito taxonomic catalogs, including the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU).

Anopheles strodei is a valid species within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus, belonging to the Argyritarsis section and the Albitarsis series. Morphological and molecular studies (COI, ITS2, and white gene) have demonstrated that what was previously considered a single species is actually a complex of several cryptic species. Revisions by Sallum et al. (2010) and Bourke et al. (2013) clarified the taxonomy of the Anopheles strodei subgroup, resulting in the description or resurrection of related taxa such as An. albertoi, An. arthuri, and An. rondoni. However, Anopheles strodei sensu stricto remains the valid name for the nominate taxon within this subgroup.

Anopheles evansae is a valid species belonging to the Argyritarsis Section, Oswaldoi Group, and Strodei Subgroup of the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. It was originally described as Cellia evansae by Brèthes in 1926. For several decades, there was taxonomic confusion between this species and Anopheles strodei; however, morphological studies of the male genitalia and larval characters, supported by molecular data, have confirmed its status as a distinct taxon. Current phylogenetic classifications maintain it within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus, although some authors propose elevating Nyssorhynchus to genus level.

Anopheles argyritarsis is the nominotypical member of the Argyritarsis Section within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. Since its original description by Robineau-Desvoidy in 1827, the species has maintained taxonomic stability, although it was historically confused with other members of the white-tarsus group (such as An. albitarsis). It is distinguished from closely related species by the pattern of scaling on the second hindtarsomere and specific male genitalia characters. It is widely distributed across the Neotropical region, from southern Mexico to northern Argentina and the Lesser Antilles.

his species was originally described by Carlos Chagas in 1908 under the name Myzorhynchella parva, based on specimens collected in Brazil. Following the taxonomic revision of the genus Anopheles and the dissolution of Myzorhynchella as a separate genus, the species was reassigned. It is currently placed within the subgenus Lophopodomyia Antunes, 1937. The validity of the species and its current taxonomic position are supported by the morphological characteristics of the adult female wing scales and male genitalia (Chagas, 1908; Lane, 1953).

The species was originally described by Francis Metcalf Root in 1926 based on specimens collected in Brazil. It is classified within the family Culicidae, subfamily Anophelinae, genus Anopheles, and subgenus Nyssorhynchus. It belongs to the Argyritarsis Section and the Darlingi Series. Although some recent molecular phylogenies have proposed elevating Nyssorhynchus to the genus level (Foster et al., 2017), the taxonomic standard maintained by the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU) and major Neotropical mosquito databases continues to recognize it as a subgenus within Anopheles (Root, 1926; Harbach, 2024).

Originally described by Peryassú (1922) as Cellia oswaldoi, the species was subsequently moved to the genus Anopheles and the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. Modern taxonomic revisions and molecular analyses have identified that Anopheles oswaldoi is a species complex (sensu lato) comprising at least four to seven cryptic species across South and Central America. The name remains valid for the taxon described from the type locality in Brazil, while other members of the complex are often referred to as species A, B, or under specific names like An. oswaldoi s.s. (Motoki et al., 2007; Ruiz-Lopez et al., 2013).

Anopheles fluminensis is a valid species belonging to the Arribalzagia Series of the subgenus Anopheloides. It was originally described by Root (1927) based on specimens collected in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Morphologically, it is closely related to Anopheles intermedius, but it can be distinguished by specific patterns in the wing maculation and male genitalia characteristics (specifically the structure of the ventral lobe of the claspette). While some historical confusion existed within the Arribalzagia series, modern integrated taxonomy (morphological and molecular) maintains its status as a distinct evolutionary lineage.

The species was originally described as Chagasia triannulata by Neiva and Pinto in 1922. It was later reassigned to the genus Anopheles and placed within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. Morphological and molecular studies have identified it as a species complex (Anopheles triannulatus complex), which currently includes An. triannulatus s.s., An. halophylus, and An. homunculus. According to the internal classification of the Nyssorhynchus subgenus, it belongs to the Argyritarsis Section and the Albimanus Series. The validity of the name is maintained in the most recent taxonomic catalogs of Culicidae (Harbach, 2024).

The species was formally described by Causey, Deane, and Deane (1943) based on specimens collected in the state of Acre, Brazil. The identification was primarily supported by the distinct morphology of the eggs and male genitalia. It is classified within the Nyssorhynchus subgenus, specifically within the Albimanus Section. Taxonomic revisions, such as those by Faran (1980), have upheld its status as a valid species, distinguishing it from closely related taxa like Anopheles goeldii and Anopheles inamollae based on wing spot patterns and larval chaetotaxy.

Anopheles rondoni is a valid species originally described as Cellia rondoni by Neiva and Pinto (1922). It belongs to the Argyritarsis Section of the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. The species is morphologically distinguished from closely related taxa, such as Anopheles strodei and Anopheles darlingi, by the presence of a characteristic dark spot at the base of the third hindtarsomere and specific wing macula patterns. Its taxonomic status as a distinct species has been upheld through morphological revisions and molecular phylogenetic analyses (Forattini, 2002; Bourke et al., 2013).

The species was formally described by Arnoldo Gabaldón in 1940. It is currently recognized as a species complex (Anopheles nuneztovari sensu lato), which includes several morphologically similar but genetically distinct lineages, such as Anopheles nuneztovari s.s., An. goeldii, and An. dunhami. Despite the ongoing taxonomic refinements using molecular tools, Anopheles nuneztovari remains a valid and widely accepted name for this group of significant Neotropical malaria vectors (Gabaldón, 1940; Conn et al., 1993).

The species was originally described by Oswaldo G. Cruz in 1901. It belongs to the subgenus Kerteszia, a group of Neotropical mosquitoes whose larvae typically develop in the water held by bromeliads. Historically, there was taxonomic confusion involving Anopheles lutzii Theobald, 1901; however, Theobald's name is considered a junior homonym and is often treated as a synonym of Anopheles (Nyssorhynchus) albitarsis or associated with Anopheles cruzii. The name Anopheles (Kerteszia) lutzii Cruz, 1901 remains the valid nomenclature for this specific taxon within the Kerteszia subgenus (Zavortink, 1973).

The species was originally described by Chagas (1907) as Cellia braziliensis. It was subsequently reassigned to the genus Anopheles and placed within the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. It belongs to the Argyritarsis Section and the Braziliensis Series. While some recent phylogenies proposed elevating Nyssorhynchus to genus rank (Foster et al., 2017), the consensus in many applied entomological frameworks remains the use of Anopheles (Nyssorhynchus) braziliensis. The species is morphologically distinct, particularly in the larval and pupal stages, and is recognized as a valid taxonomic entity in the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU) databases and the Systematic Catalog of Culicidae.

The genus Anopheles was established by Johann Wilhelm Meigen in 1818. It is the type genus of the subfamily Anophelinae (Family: Culicidae). Currently, the genus comprises over 460 formally recognized species and numerous species complexes. The designation "spp." is a collective botanical and zoological abbreviation used to refer to multiple species within this genus when individual identification is not specified or required. Taxonomically, the genus is divided into several subgenera, including Anopheles, Cellia, Kerteszia, Lophopodomyia, Nyssorhynchus, and Stethomyia (Meigen, 1818; Harbach, 2013).

Anopheles mediopunctatus was originally described by Lutz (1910) as Cycloleppteron mediopunctatus. It is currently recognized as the type species of the subgenus Lophopodomyia Antunes, 1937. The species status was clarified and revalidated through a comprehensive taxonomic revision of the subgenus Lophopodomyia conducted by Sallum, Wilkerson, and Forattini (2000). This revision utilized morphological characters of the male genitalia, larvae, and pupae to distinguish An. mediopunctatus from closely related and often misidentified species such as An. costai and An. forattinii.

Anopheles minor was formally described by Costa Lima (1929) based on specimens collected in Brazil. It is a valid species within the subgenus Lophopodomyia. Taxonomic stability for this taxon is maintained through the morphological characterization of the adult stage, particularly the male genitalia and the thoracic scales, which distinguish it from other species in the same subgenus, such as An. gilesi (Costa Lima, 1929; Lane, 1953).

The species was formally described by Galvão and Amaral (1938) based on specimens collected from the state of São Paulo, Brazil. It is taxonomically situated within the Argyritarsis Section of the subgenus Nyssorhynchus. While some recent phylogenetic classifications (Foster et al., 2017) propose elevating Nyssorhynchus to the genus level, the name Anopheles lanei remains the standard reference in most entomological and medical literature within the traditional classification framework.

Anopheles antunesi is recognized as a valid species belonging to the subgenus Lophopodomyia. It was originally described by Galvão and Amaral (1940) based on specimens collected in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. The species is morphologically distinct within its subgenus, particularly characterized by the scaling patterns on the legs and specific male genitalia structures. Its taxonomic status has been maintained in major revisions of the Anophelinae subfamily (Knight & Stone, 1977; Harbach, 2004).

Anopheles gilesi was originally described by Peryassú in 1908. It is currently recognized as a valid species belonging to the subgenus Anopheles, specifically within the Arribalzagia Series. This series is characterized by specific wing spot patterns and male genitalic features. Taxonomic stability has been maintained through various revisions of the Neotropical Anopheles fauna, confirming its distinct morphological identity from closely related species such as Anopheles intermedius and Anopheles punctimacula (Peryassú, 1908; Wilkerson & Sallum, 1999).

This species was formally described and established by Causey, Deane, and Deane (1945) based on morphological characteristics observed in specimens from Ceará, Brazil. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the genus Chagasia (Subfamily Anophelinae). Unlike other members of the subfamily, the genus Chagasia is considered more primitive, and C. rozeboomi is distinguished from its congeners (such as C. bathana or C. fajardi) by specific patterns in the wing scales and male genitalia.

This taxon is frequently confused with Chagasia rozeboomi Gabaldón et al., 1940. Causey et al. described only an Anopheles in 1944. Any attribution by Causey to the genus Chagasia is a bibliographic error. The Anopheles status is maintained for specimens from project PINV01-528 collected in malaria transmission areas.

The species was originally described as Anopheles lutzii by Oswaldo Cruz in 1901. It is currently recognized as the type species of the subgenus Myzorhynchella Theobald. There has been historical nomenclatural confusion with Anopheles lutzi Theobald, 1901; however, Theobald's name is considered a junior secondary homonym and a synonym of Anopheles (Kerteszia) cruzii Dyar & Knab, 1908. In contrast, Anopheles lutzii Cruz, 1901 remains a valid and distinct taxon within the Myzorhynchella Series (Wilkerson & Sallum, 1999).

This taxon is frequently confused with Chagasia rozeboomi Gabaldón et al., 1940. Causey et al. described only an Anopheles in 1944. Any attribution by Causey to the genus Chagasia is a bibliographic error. The Anopheles status is maintained for specimens from project PINV01-528 collected in malaria transmission areas.

The genus Anopheles was established by Johann Wilhelm Meigen in 1818. It is currently the most significant genus within the subfamily Anophelinae (Family: Culicidae). The classification is based on morphological characteristics such as the length of the maxillary palps in both sexes (roughly equal to the proboscis) and the absence of a trilobed scutellum. This taxonomic status is consistently validated in the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory (Harbach, 2024), maintaining its position as a monophyletic group comprising seven subgenera: Anopheles, Bironella, Christya, Kerteszia, Lophopodomyia, Nyssorhynchus, and Stethomyia.

The species was originally described as Culex scapularis by Rondani in 1848. For much of the 20th century, it was classified within the genus Aedes. Following the taxonomic reclassification proposed by Reinert (2000), the subgenus Ochlerotatus was elevated to generic rank, leading to the combination Ochlerotatus scapularis. However, subsequent phylogenetic analyses and a push for taxonomic stability led Wilkerson et al. (2015) to propose returning Ochlerotatus to subgeneric status within Aedes. Currently, most international databases and entomological authorities, such as the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU), recognize the valid name as Aedes scapularis.

The genus Anopheles was established by Johann Wilhelm Meigen in 1818. It is currently the most significant genus within the subfamily Anophelinae (Family: Culicidae). The classification is based on morphological characteristics such as the length of the maxillary palps in both sexes (roughly equal to the proboscis) and the absence of a trilobed scutellum. This taxonomic status is consistently validated in the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory (Harbach, 2024), maintaining its position as a monophyletic group comprising seven subgenera: Anopheles, Bironella, Christya, Kerteszia, Lophopodomyia, Nyssorhynchus, and Stethomyia.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus longipalpis by Lutz and Neiva in 1912 based on specimens collected in Brazil. It was later reassigned to the genus Lutzomyia by França (1924) and remains the type species of the genus. Current taxonomic consensus acknowledges that Lutzomyia longipalpis represents a complex of sibling species rather than a single monotypic taxon, evidenced by variations in male pheromones, acoustic signals, and molecular markers (Arrivillaga & Feliciangeli, 2001). However, until these members are formally described as individual species, Lutzomyia longipalpis remains the valid taxonomic name used in medical and entomological literature.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus neivai by Pinto (1926). For several decades, it was considered a junior synonym of Nyssomyia intermedia (Lutz & Neiva, 1912). However, Marcondes (1996) conducted a detailed morphological and morphometric revision of the intermedia complex, resurrecting Nyssomyia neivai (formerly Lutzomyia neivai) as a valid species. The classification under the genus Nyssomyia follows the taxonomic arrangement proposed by Galati (2003), based on phylogenetic analyses of the subtribe Psychodopygina.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus shannoni by Dyar in 1929. Following the taxonomic revisions of the subfamily Phlebotominae, it was long included in the genus Lutzomyia, subgenus Psathyromyia (Young & Duncan, 1994). However, current phylogenetic classifications and morphological revisions (Galati, 2003; 2018) have elevated Psathyromyia Barretto, 1962 to generic rank. Therefore, the valid combination is Psathyromyia (Psathyromyia) shannoni (Dyar, 1929).

Originally described by Larrousse (1920) under the name Phlebotomus brumpti based on specimens collected in Brazil. The species was later assigned as the type species of the genus Brumptomyia by França and Parrot (1921). The taxonomic status is widely accepted in modern Neotropical sand fly classification systems (Galati, 2003; Young & Duncan, 1994), which distinguish Brumptomyia from Lutzomyia based on the morphology of the male genitalia (specifically the presence of a basal tuft of setae on the coxite) and the cibarium in females.

Originally described as Phlebotomus migonei by França (1920) based on specimens collected in Paraguay. It was later reassigned to the genus Migonemyia by Galati (1995) during the phylogenetic reclassification of the subtribe Lutzomyiina. The species is the type species of the genus Migonemyia and is widely recognized under this binomen in current Neotropical dipterology (Galati, 2021).

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus whitmani by Antunes and Coutinho (1939). It was later included in the genus Lutzomyia, subgenus Nyssomyia. Following the phylogenetic classification system proposed by Galati (2003), the subgenus Nyssomyia was elevated to the rank of genus. This taxonomic status is widely accepted in modern Neotropical dipterology and is supported by morphological and molecular evidence that distinguishes the Nyssomyia lineage from other Phlebotominae groups.

The species was originally described by Costa Lima in 1932 under the binomen Phlebotomus avellari. Following the taxonomic restructuring of the subfamily Phlebotominae, specifically the elevation of Brumptomyia to generic status and the re-evaluation of morphological characters (such as the presence of a row of longitudinal setae on the male style), the species was formally reassigned to the genus Brumptomyia. This classification is currently upheld in the major taxonomic catalogs of Neotropical sand flies (Young & Duncan, 1994; Galati, 2003).

Originally described as Phlebotomus whitmani by Antunes and Coutinho (1939). It was subsequently included in the genus Lutzomyia, subgenus Nyssomyia, by various authors (Young & Duncan, 1994). Following the taxonomic reclassification of the subfamily Phlebotominae proposed by Galati (2003), the subgenus Nyssomyia was elevated to the genus level. This classification is currently the standard for Neotropical sand fly studies under project PINV01-528, confirming the valid name as Nyssomyia whitmani.

Originally described as Phlebotomus evandroi by Costa Lima and Antunes (1936) based on specimens collected in São Paulo, Brazil. The species was later reassigned to the genus Evandromyia Mangabeira, 1941. Under the classification system proposed by Galati (2003), it is the type species of the genus Evandromyia and belongs to the subgenus Evandromyia. The classification is justified by the morphological characteristics of the male terminalia (specifically the structure of the paramere and aedeagus) and the female spermathecae, which distinguish it from species in the genus Lutzomyia.

Originally described as Phlebotomus guimaraesi by Coutinho and Barretto (1941) based on specimens collected in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. The species was later transferred to the genus Brumptomyia (França & Parrot, 1921) as part of the taxonomic reorganization of the Neotropical Phlebotominae, which separated species associated with armadillo burrows and specific morphological traits (e.g., ascoid shape and male genitalia structure) from the genus Lutzomyia sensu lato. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the Brumptomyina subtribe (Galati, 2003; Shimabukuro et al., 2017).

Originally described as Phlebotomus neivai by Pinto (1926), this species was long considered a junior synonym of Lutzomyia intermedia. However, Marcondes (1996) revalidated the species based on morphological differences in the female spermathecae and male terminalia, establishing the intermedia complex. Under the phylogenetic classification system proposed by Galati (2003), which is widely adopted in the Neotropics and supported by the PINV01-528 project framework, the subgenus Nyssomyia was elevated to the genus level. Therefore, the currently accepted combination is Nyssomyia neivai.

The species was originally described by Brèthes (1923) under the genus Phlebotomus as Phlebotomus cortelezzii. Following the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003), it was placed within the genus Evandromyia Mangabeira, 1941, subgenus Evandromyia. It is the nominate species of the cortelezzii complex, which also includes E. sallesi and E. corumbaensis. The identification of females within this complex is particularly challenging due to high morphological similarity, often requiring the use of molecular tools or the association with sympatric males for definitive diagnostic resolution.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus pessoai by Coutinho and Barretto (1940). For several decades, it was widely classified under the genus Lutzomyia (subgenus Pintomyia). However, according to the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003), which is extensively utilized in Neotropical sand fly studies, the subgenus Pintomyia was elevated to the status of genus. Therefore, the current valid name is Pintomyia (Pintomyia) pessoai (Coutinho & Barretto, 1940). This classification is supported by the morphological characteristics of the male genitalia (five long spines on the style and a short, thick paramere) and the female spermathecae.

The genus Brumptomyia was established by França and Parrot (1921) to accommodate species previously classified under Phlebotomus that exhibited distinct morphological characteristics in the male genitalia, specifically the presence of a basal tuft of setae on the gonocoxite and a simplified paramere structure. The type species is Phlebotomus brumpti Larrousse, 1920. In modern Neotropical sand fly taxonomy, Brumptomyia is recognized as a valid genus within the tribe Phlebotomini, supported by comprehensive phylogenetic and morphological revisions (Galati, 2003; 2018; Young & Duncan, 1994).

La especie fue descrita originalmente por Mangabeira en 1938 bajo el nombre de Flebotomus lenti. Posteriormente, fue transferida al género Lutzomyia y clasificada dentro del subgénero Evandromyia por Young y Duncan (1994). Sin embargo, siguiendo la clasificación filogenética propuesta por Galati (2003), el subgénero fue elevado a nivel de género, estableciéndose el nombre actual como Evandromyia lenti. Esta clasificación es la más aceptada en los estudios taxonómicos contemporáneos de la fauna de flebotominos neotropicales.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus shannoni by Dyar (1929). It was later transferred to the genus Lutzomyia and eventually placed within the genus Psathyromyia based on the taxonomic revisions proposed by Barretto (1962). The current classification follows the phylogenetic and morphological criteria established by Galati (2003, 2018), which treats Psathyromyia as a distinct genus within the subtribe Psychodopygina. The species is the type species of the genus Psathyromyia.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus pessoai by Coutinho and Barretto (1940). It was subsequently included in the genus Lutzomyia, subgenus Pintomyia, by various authors during the late 20th century (Young & Duncan, 1994). Following the phylogenetic reclassification of the Phlebotominae subfamily proposed by Galati (2003), the subgenus Pintomyia was elevated to the status of a genus. Pintomyia pessoai is currently recognized as the type species of the pessoai series within the subgenus Pintomyia (Galati, 2021).

The genus Evandromyia was originally established by Mangabeira (1941) as a subgenus of Flebotomus. It was later elevated to genus status and redefined within the subtribe Psychodopygina by Galati (2003). Currently, it is subdivided into three subgenera: Evandromyia s. str., Aldamyia Galati, 1995, and Barrettomyia Martins & Silva, 1968. This taxonomic arrangement is widely accepted in Neotropical dipterology to categorize a specific group of sand flies characterized by the morphology of the spermathecae and the male genitalia (Galati, 2003; Shimabukuro et al., 2017).

This species was originally described under the genus Phlebotomus by Forattini in 1954, based on specimens collected in Chile. Following the taxonomic restructuring of the Neotropical Phlebotominae, Galati (2003) placed the species within the genus Pintomyia Costa Lima, 1932, specifically in the nominate subgenus Pintomyia. This classification has been maintained in subsequent phylogenetic and taxonomic updates (Galati, 2018; 2021) and is the current standard for the project PINV01-528.

The species was originally described under the name Psychodopygus carmelinoi by Ryan, Fraiha, Lainson, and Shaw (1986) from specimens collected in the state of Pará, Brazil. Following the taxonomic reclassification of the subtribe Lutzomyiina, the species was transferred to the genus Evandromyia Mangabeira, 1941, and placed within the subgenus Aldamyia Galati, 1995. This placement is justified by morphological characteristics of the male terminalia and the female spermathecae, which align with the Aldamyia series as defined by Galati (2003).

Originally described as Phlebotomus intermedius by Lutz and Neiva (1912). The species was later included in the genus Lutzomyia as Lutzomyia intermedia. However, following the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003), which is the standard for the PINV01-528 project, the species is currently placed in the genus Nyssomyia Barretto, 1962. This classification is based on specific morphological characters of the spermathecae in females and the terminalia in males. It is considered the type species of the genus Nyssomyia.

Originally described as Phlebotomus termitophilus by Martins, Falcão & Silva (1964), this species was later reassigned to the genus Evandromyia, subgenus Aldemyia, following the phylogenetic classification system established by Galati (2003). The classification is based on specific morphological characters of the male genitalia (specifically the parameres and aedeagus) and the female spermathecae, which align with the Aldemyia series within the Evandromyia lineage.

The species was originally described by Pinto (1926) as Phlebotomus fischeri. While it was traditionally classified under the genus Lutzomyia for several decades, the current taxonomic stability follows the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003). Galati elevated the subgenus Pintomyia (Costa Lima, 1932) to the rank of genus, placing this species within the nominate subgenus. This classification is widely accepted in Neotropical dipterology and used by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO).

Originally described as Phlebotomus quinquefer by Dyar (1929). In the classification system proposed by Young and Duncan (1994), it was treated as Lutzomyia (Micropygomyia) quinquefer. However, following the phylogenetic classification by Galati (2003), which was updated and consolidated in Galati (2018), Micropygomyia Barretto, 1962 was elevated to the status of a genus. The species is currently recognized under the nominate subgenus Micropygomyia.

The species was originally described by Costa Lima in 1932 as Phlebotomus monticolus. Following the taxonomic reorganization of the subfamily Phlebotominae, it was transferred to the genus Lutzomyia França, 1924. According to the classification systems of Young and Duncan (1994) and Galati (2003, 2018), the species is valid and serves as the type species for the monticola series within the subgenus Lutzomyia. The species is characterized by its distinct paramere structure and spermathecae morphology in the female.

La especie fue descrita originalmente por Mangabeira en 1938 bajo el nombre de Phlebotomus lenti. Posteriormente, tras las revisiones taxonómicas de la subfamilia Phlebotominae, fue transferida al género Evandromyia Mangabeira, 1941. Según la clasificación filogenética propuesta por Galati (2003, 2021), se ubica dentro del subgénero Evandromyia, basándose en la morfología característica del cibario en las hembras (presencia de dientes horizontales y verticales bien desarrollados) y la estructura de los parámetros y el edeago en los machos.

Originally described as Phlebotomus fischeri by Pinto (1926), the species was later reassigned to the genus Lutzomyia. However, following the phylogenetic reclassification of the subfamily Phlebotominae by Galati (2003), the species is currently recognized under the genus Pintomyia Costa Lima, 1932, and the subgenus Pintomyia. This taxonomic status is maintained in recent systematic revisions of Neotropical sand flies (Galati, 2018).

Originally described as Phlebotomus quinquefer by Dyar (1929). In the classification system proposed by Young and Duncan (1994), it was treated as Lutzomyia (Micropygomyia) quinquefer. However, following the phylogenetic classification by Galati (2003), which was updated and consolidated in Galati (2018), Micropygomyia Barretto, 1962 was elevated to the status of a genus. The species is currently recognized under the nominate subgenus Micropygomyia.

The species was originally described by Mangabeira (1942) under the binomen Phlebotomus cunhai. It was later reassigned to the genus Brumptomyia França & Parrot, 1921, following the taxonomic restructuring of the subfamily Phlebotominae. The genus Brumptomyia is morphologically distinguished by males possessing a coxite with a basal tuft of long setae and parameres with specific arrangements of spines. Taxonomic revisions by Galati (2003, 2018) confirm the validity of this species within the Brumptomyia genus based on these diagnostic genital characters.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus migonei by França (1920). It was later widely cited under the genus Lutzomyia following the classification of Young and Duncan (1994). However, the currently accepted taxonomic arrangement for the project PINV01-528 follows Galati (1995, 2003), who elevated several subgenera to generic status based on phylogenetic analyses. Under this system, the species is placed within the genus Migonemyia Galati, 1995, as the type species of the genus. The spelling "Mygonemyia" is a common orthographic error; the correct nomenclature is Migonemyia (Galati, 1995).

Originally described as Flebotomus cruzi by Mangabeira (1938), this species is a member of the Lutzomyia longipalpis species complex within the subgenus Lutzomyia França, 1924. It is morphologically similar to Lu. longipalpis, but males can be distinguished by the shorter length of the paramere and the arrangement of the setae on the coxite. Its status as a distinct species is supported by morphological, biochemical, and molecular data (Young & Duncan, 1994; Galati, 2003).

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus puntigeniculatus by Floch and Abonnenc (1944) based on specimens collected in French Guiana. It was later included in the genus Lutzomyia as Lutzomyia puntigeniculata within the shannoni species group (Young & Duncan, 1994). Following the taxonomic reclassification of the Phlebotominae by Galati (2003), the species was transferred to the genus Psathyromyia Barretto, 1962, and placed within the subgenus Psathyromyia. This classification remains the current consensus in Neotropical dipterology (Galati, 2018; Galati, 2021).

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus misionensis by Castro (1959) from specimens collected in the Misiones Province, Argentina. It was later included in the genus Lutzomyia under the subgenus Pintomyia. Following the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003), the subgenus Pintomyia Costa Lima, 1932 was elevated to the status of genus. Currently, Pintomyia misionensis is recognized as a valid species within the tribe Phlebotomini, subtribe Lutzomyiina (Galati, 2018).

Originally described as Phlebotomus neivai by Pinto (1926), this species was long considered a junior synonym of Nyssomyia intermedia (Lutz & Neiva, 1912). However, it was resurrected as a valid species by Marcondes (1996) based on detailed morphological analyses of the spermathecae in females and the parameres in males. Under the classification system proposed by Galati (2003), the species is placed within the genus Nyssomyia Barretto, 1962. It is a member of the intermedia complex, and its taxonomic status is widely accepted in current Neotropical dipterology (Galati, 2018).

The genus Brumptomyia was established by França and Parrot (1921) to classify a group of Neotropical phlebotomine sand flies that were morphologically distinct from the genus Phlebotomus. It is recognized as a valid monophyletic genus within the subfamily Phlebotominae. Morphologically, males are distinguished by having a basal tuft of setae on the gonocoxite and relatively complex parameres, while females possess spermathecae with distinct neck-like structures and long individual ducts. According to Young and Duncan (1994), Brumptomyia species are restricted to the New World, ranging from the southern United States to northern Argentina, and are taxonomically separated from Lutzomyia sensu lato by their specific ecological niches and genital morphology.

Originally described as Phlebotomus migonei by França (1920), the species was later included in the genus Lutzomyia. According to the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (1995, 2003), it was reclassified into the genus Migonemyia. The use of the trinomial Migonemyia migonei migonei is considered obsolete in current dipterology; the species is recognized as monotypic throughout its wide distribution in South America (from Colombia to Argentina). Therefore, the repetition of the specific epithet as a subspecies is taxonomically redundant and not supported by current morphological or molecular evidence.

La especie fue descrita originalmente por Mangabeira en 1938 bajo el nombre Flebotomus lenti. Posteriormente, tras las revisiones taxonómicas de la familia Psychodidae, subfamilia Phlebotominae, fue transferida al género Evandromyia establecido por el mismo autor en 1941. De acuerdo con la clasificación filogenética propuesta por Galati (2003, 2018) y ampliamente aceptada en la región neotropical, se ubica en el subgénero Evandromyia, serie lenti. El uso del nombre subespecífico (trinominal) es actualmente redundante en la literatura técnica moderna, prefiriéndose el binomio Evandromyia lenti, a menos que se realicen estudios comparativos con poblaciones geográficamente aisladas que justifiquen una subdivisión subespecífica.

The taxon was originally described as Phlebotomus longipalpis by Lutz and Neiva in 1912. It was later reassigned to the genus Lutzomyia following the taxonomic revisions that separated New World sand flies from the Old World genus Phlebotomus. According to the classification system proposed by Galati (2003), it belongs to the subgenus Lutzomyia. Although the trinomial Lutzomyia longipalpis longipalpis has been used in the past to denote the nominate subspecies, contemporary teaxonomy and molecular evidence suggest that L. longipalpis is a species complex (sensu lato) rather than a group of subspecies. Therefore, the binomial Lutzomyia longipalpis is the currently accepted valid name for the species (Young & Duncan, 1994; Galati, 2018).

The taxon was originally described as Phlebotomus neivai by Pinto (1926). Following the taxonomic revisions of the subtribe Psychodopygina, it was placed within the genus Lutzomyia and later transferred to the genus Nyssomyia (Galati, 2003). Although sometimes referred to with a trinomial name in older literature or specific regional contexts, modern Phlebotominae systematics treats Nyssomyia neivai as a monotypic species. It was resurrected from synonymy with Nyssomyia intermedia by Marcondes (1996), who established morphological and bio-ecological differences between the two species, a distinction further supported by molecular studies and formal redescription (Andrade Filho et al., 2003).

Originally described as Phlebotomus cortelezzii (Brèthes, 1923), the species was later reassigned to the genus Lutzomyia and subsequently to Evandromyia under the subgenus Evandromyia, following the taxonomic stability provided by Galati (2003). The use of the trinomial Evandromyia cortelezzii cortelezzii is considered obsolete in modern classification; current Neotropical dipterology treats it as a species within the cortelezzii complex. This complex includes E. cortelezzii, E. sallesi, and E. corumbaensis, where females are often morphologically indistinguishable, requiring the binomial nomenclature supported by Galati (2021).

Originally described as Phlebotomus puntigeniculatus by Floch and Abonnenc in 1944. It was later placed within the genus Lutzomyia, subgenus Psathyromyia. According to the phylogenetic classification proposed by Galati (2003), the subgenus Psathyromyia was elevated to generic status. The use of the trinomial Psathyromyia puntigeniculata puntigeniculata is currently deprecated in modern taxonomic revisions, as the subspecies distinctions within this taxon are not widely recognized or supported by morphological and molecular evidence. Therefore, the species is treated as a single taxon: Psathyromyia (Psathyromyia) puntigeniculata (Galati, 2018; 2021).

The taxon was originally described as Phlebotomus brumpti by Larrousse (1920). It was later moved to the genus Brumptomyia, established by França & Parrot (1921), of which it is the type species. In modern Neotropical Phlebotominae taxonomy, the use of trinomial nomenclature for this species is considered redundant or obsolete. According to the classification systems proposed by Young & Duncan (1994) and updated by Galati (2018), the species is recognized as Brumptomyia brumpti. The nominate subspecies Brumptomyia brumpti brumpti is treated simply as a synonym of the species, as no valid subspecies are currently recognized within this taxon.

Originally described as Phlebotomus cortelezzii by Brethes (1923), the species was later reassigned to the genus Evandromyia, subgenus Aldamyia, following the phylogenetic and morphological classification established by Galati (2003). The use of the trinomial Evandromyia cortelezzii cortelezzii is considered outdated in modern Neotropical dipterology; the taxon is currently recognized at the species level. It belongs to the "cortelezzii complex," which also includes E. sallesi and E. corumbaensis. This complex is characterized by the morphological similarity of females, which are often indistinguishable, requiring male terminalia for definitive specific identification (Galati, 2021).

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus avellari by Costa Lima (1932). It was subsequently transferred to the genus Brumptomyia by Theodor (1948). The use of the trinomial Brumptomyia avellari avellari was used in older classifications to distinguish the nominate subspecies; however, modern taxonomic revisions and phylogenetic catalogs (Galati, 2003; Galati, 2018; Shimabukuro et al., 2017) do not recognize valid subspecies for this taxon, treating the name as Brumptomyia avellari.

The taxon was originally described as Phlebotomus whitmani by Antunes and Coutinho in 1939. It was later transferred to the genus Nyssomyia following the classification systems of Barretto (1962) and subsequently Galati (2003). The use of the trinomial Nyssomyia whitmani whitmani is considered taxonomically redundant and obsolete in modern Neotropical sand fly nomenclature, as there are currently no recognized or valid subspecies within this taxon. According to the phylogenetic and morphological revisions by Galati (2003, 2018), the species is treated as a monotypic binomen.

The species was originally described as Phlebotomus kuscheli by Forattini (1954) from specimens collected in Chile. Following the taxonomic restructuring of the subfamily Phlebotominae by Galati (2003), the species was reassigned to the genus Pintomyia Costa Lima, 1932, and the subgenus Pintomyia. The use of the trinomial Pintomyia kuscheli kuscheli refers to the nominate subspecies; however, in most modern taxonomic checklists (Galati, 2018; 2021), it is treated at the species level as Pintomyia kuscheli unless specifically differentiating from other described subspecies within its range.

The species was originally described by Stål in 1859 under the binomen Conorhinus sordidus. It was later transferred to the genus Triatoma. It is currently recognized as a valid species and serves as the head of the Triatoma sordida subcomplex. Taxonomical stability has been maintained through morphological and molecular characterization, which distinguishes it from cryptic or closely related species such as Triatoma rosai and Triatoma garciabesi (Galvão et al., 2003; Alevi et al., 2020).

Triatoma guasayana was described by Wygodzinsky and Abalos in 1949. It is recognized as a valid species within the Triatoma infestans subcomplex. Morphologically, it is closely related to T. sordida and T. patagonica, but it can be distinguished by specific features of the male genitalia and its distinct chromatic patterns. Its status as a separate biological entity has been confirmed through various taxonomic revisions and molecular phylogenetic analyses (Carcavallo et al., 1999; Galvão et al., 2003).

The species was originally described by Johann Christoph Friedrich Klug in 1834 under the binomen Reduvius infestans. It was later reassigned to the genus Triatoma Laporte, 1832. This species is the type species of the "infestans subcomplex" within the Triatoma infestans complex. Its taxonomic status is well-established and stable based on morphological characters of the head, thorax, and male genitalia, as detailed in the revision of the subfamily Triatominae by Lent & Wygodzinsky (1979).

Originally described by Hermann Burmeister in 1835 under the binomen Conorhinus megistus. The species was later transferred to the genus Panstrongylus Berg, 1879. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the tribe Triatomini. The taxonomic status is stable, supported by morphological characterization of the head (short and robust) and the location of the antennal insertion near the eyes (Lent & Wygodzinsky, 1979).

Originally described by Latreille (1811) as Reduvius geniculatus based on specimens from French Guiana. It was later moved to the genus Panstrongylus Berg, 1879. This species serves as the type species for the genus Panstrongylus. Its taxonomic status was extensively reviewed and confirmed by Lent & Wygodzinsky (1979) in their definitive revision of the subfamily Triatominae.

Triatoma guasu was formally described by Herman Lent and Pedro Wygodzinsky in 1979 during their comprehensive revision of the subfamily Triatominae. The species was identified based on specimens collected in Paraguay. Taxonomically, it is integrated into the Triatoma infestans species group (specifically the T. infestans subcomplex). It is morphologically characterized by its large size (from which its specific epithet "guasu," meaning "big" in Guaraní, is derived) and distinct male genitalic structures. Its status as a valid species has been consistently upheld in subsequent checklists and phylogenetic studies (Galvão et al., 2003; Justi & Galvão, 2017).

Triatoma platensis was formally described by Arthur Neiva in 1913. It belongs to the Triatoma infestans subcomplex (within the infestans complex). The species is morphologically and genetically distinct but maintains a high degree of evolutionary proximity to T. infestans, with which it can produce fertile hybrids under both laboratory and natural conditions in areas of sympatry. Its taxonomic status as a valid species is supported by morphometric analysis and molecular markers (Lent & Wygodzinsky, 1979; Dujardin et al., 2000; Galvão et al., 2003).

The genus Rhodnius was established by Carl Stål in 1859. It is currently recognized as a valid genus within the tribe Rhodniini of the subfamily Triatominae (Hemiptera: Reduviidae). Taxonomically, the genus is distinguished from other triatomines by the insertion of the antennae at the anterior extremity of the head (near the apex) and the presence of postocular callosities. The monophyly of the genus has been supported by both classical morphological revisions (Lent & Wygodzinsky, 1979) and modern molecular phylogenetic analyses (Galvão et al., 2003; Justi & Galvão, 2017).

The genus Triatoma was established by Laporte in 1832. It is currently recognized as the most diverse genus within the subfamily Triatominae (Hemiptera: Reduviidae), comprising approximately 80 valid species. It serves as the type genus for the tribe Triatomini. Systematic studies based on morphological and molecular data continue to support its validity, although some subgeneric arrangements and species complexes (such as the Triatoma phyllosoma or Triatoma brasiliensis complexes) are subject to ongoing taxonomic refinement (Lent & Wygodzinsky, 1979; Galvão et al., 2003).

The species was originally described as Culex aegypti by Linnaeus in 1762. Over time, it was reassigned to the genus Aedes. Although Reinert et al. (2004) proposed elevating the subgenus Stegomyia to genus level (which would change the name to Stegomyia aegypti), the wider scientific community, particularly in medical entomology, opted to maintain the traditional classification to ensure nomenclatural stability. This position was solidified by Wilkerson et al. (2015), who argued for the retention of Aedes to avoid confusion in public health and clinical literature.

The species was originally described as Haemagogus spegazzinii by Juan Brèthes in 1912 based on specimens collected in Argentina. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the subgenus Haemagogus. Taxonomic stability was reinforced by Arnell (1973) in his comprehensive revision of the genus, where he clarified the morphological distinctions between H. spegazzinii and the closely related H. capricornii, based on male genitalia and larval characters (Brethés, 1912; Arnell, 1973).

The name Psorophora janthinosoma and Psorophora spegazzinii are historical taxonomic treatments that have been resolved through synonymy. Originally described as Culex ferox by Humboldt (1819), the species was later moved to the genus Psorophora, subgenus Janthinosoma. Psorophora spegazzinii (Blanchard, 1905) was once considered a distinct species or subspecies but was definitively synonymized with Psorophora ferox based on morphological consistency across its range in the Americas (Knight & Stone, 1977). The term "janthinosoma" is currently recognized as the subgeneric rank, not a specific epithet for this taxon.

The name Ochlerotatus chrysoconops fulvus is a taxonomic combination of synonyms. The species was originally described as Culex fulvus by Wiedemann in 1828. The name Culex chrysoconops Wiedemann, 1821 is considered a junior synonym of Aedes fulvus. Following the phylogenetic revisions by Reinert (2000), Ochlerotatus was elevated to generic rank; however, subsequent consensus and the comprehensive reclassification by Wilkerson et al. (2015) treat Ochlerotatus as a subgenus within the genus Aedes. Therefore, the valid name for this taxon is Aedes (Ochlerotatus) fulvus (Wiedemann, 1828).

The species was originally described as Culex scapularis by Rondani (1848). While Reinert et al. (2004) elevated the subgenus Ochlerotatus to the rank of genus, subsequent comprehensive phylogenetic and taxonomic reviews led by Wilkerson et al. (2015) argued for the restoration of Ochlerotatus as a subgenus within the genus Aedes. This reclassification was proposed to maintain nomenclatural stability among mosquitoes of significant medical and veterinary importance. Therefore, the valid name recognized by the international community and the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU) is Aedes scapularis.

The species was originally described as Culex serratus by Theobald (1901). For much of the 20th century, it was classified under the genus Aedes, subgenus Ochlerotatus. Following the taxonomic revision by Reinert (2000), Ochlerotatus was elevated to the genus level, making the combination Ochlerotatus serratus widely used in literature. However, more recent comprehensive phylogenetic analyses and taxonomic stability efforts (Wilkerson et al., 2015) have returned Ochlerotatus to subgeneric status within the genus Aedes. Consequently, the valid name is Aedes (Ochlerotatus) serratus.

The taxon was originally described as Janicomyia albigenu by Peryassú in 1908. While historical literature sometimes treated it as a variety or synonym within the "janthinosoma" group or associated it with Psorophora albipes, modern taxonomic classifications recognize it as a valid species. The species is placed within the subgenus Janicomyia. Its status as a distinct species has been upheld in major taxonomic revisions and catalogs, including those by Lane (1953) and Knight & Stone (1977), based on distinct morphological features of the adult female and male genitalia.

The tLa especie fue descrita originalmente por Harrison G. Dyar en 1921 a partir de especímenes recolectados en Trinidad. Pertenece al subgénero Haemagogus y se distingue de otras especies del género por la morfología de la genitalia del macho y el patrón de escamas metálicas en el tórax y abdomen. La validez taxonómica de Haemagogus celeste ha sido ratificada en revisiones sistemáticas profundas de la tribu Aedini y del género en la región Neotropical (Arnell, 1973), manteniéndose como un nombre aceptado en las bases de datos zoológicas actuales.

The taxon was originally described as Sabethoides intermedius by Lutz in 1904. Subsequent taxonomic revisions by Lane (1953) and the world catalog by Knight & Stone (1977) confirmed its status as a valid species within the genus Sabethes, specifically under the subgenus Sabethoides. The combination "Sabethes sabethinus intermedius" is an obsolete trinomial or a historical misclassification; current mosquito taxonomy recognizes Sabethes intermedius (Lutz, 1904) and Sabethes sabethinus (Lutz, 1905) as two distinct, valid species. Following the Principle of Priority (ICZN), Sabethes intermedius is the correct name for the taxon described by Lutz in 1904.

The species was originally described as Culex aegypti by Linnaeus in 1762. While Reinert, Harbach, and Kitching (2004) proposed elevating the subgenus Stegomyia to the rank of genus (which would make the name Stegomyia aegypti), this change faced significant resistance from the global scientific and public health communities. To ensure nomenclatural stability and prevent confusion in epidemiological reporting, Wilkerson et al. (2015) reclassified the tribe Aedini, relegating Stegomyia back to a subgeneric level under the genus Aedes. This consensus is currently followed by major taxonomic databases and medical entomology organizations.

The taxon was originally described as a distinct species by Peryassú (1922). Although some historical classifications treated various members of the Sabethes genus with ambiguity regarding their specific or subspecific status, Sabethes quasicyaneus is currently recognized as a valid species within the subgenus Sabethes. This status is supported by morphological revisions of the genus, particularly those focusing on the male genitalia and adult ornamentation, which distinguish it from closely related taxa such as Sabethes cyaneus (Harbach, 1994).

The name Sabethes sabethoides (Surcouf & Gonzalez-Rincones, 1911) is a junior synonym of Sabethes chloropterus (Humboldt, 1819). Originally described by Humboldt as Culex chloropterus, the species was later reassigned to the genus Sabethes. The taxon sabethoides was formally synonymized under chloropterus after taxonomic revisions confirmed they represented the same biological entity, characterized by the metallic blue-green reflections and specific larval habitats in tree holes. Current nomenclature follows the World Mosquito Catalog and the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory (Harbach, 2024).

The taxon was originally described as a valid species, Sabethes glaucodaemon, by Dyar & Shannon (1925). Although historical treatments occasionally listed it as a subspecies or variety of Sabethes sabethoides, taxonomic revisions by Lane (1953) and subsequent catalogs (Knight & Stone, 1977) confirmed its status as a distinct species. Morphological characteristics, particularly in the male genitalia and the distribution of iridescent scales on the legs and thorax, distinguish it from Sa. sabethoides. It is currently classified within the subgenus Sabethes.

The taxon was originally described by Theobald (1901) as Janitinosoma lutzii. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the subgenus Janthinosoma of the genus Psorophora. The combination "Psorophora janthinosoma lutzii" is taxonomically incorrect as it treats the subgenus name as a specific epithet or part of a trinomial nomenclature. According to the current classification of the Culicidae, Psorophora lutzii is the correct specific name (Theobald, 1901; Knight & Stone, 1977).

The species was originally described by Neiva (1908) under the binomen Sabethes belisarioi. According to the current taxonomic arrangement and the World Mosquito Catalog, it is classified as a valid species within the subgenus Sabethes. The nomenclature follows the principle of priority and subsequent taxonomic stability established in major revisions of the tribe Sabethini (Knight & Stone, 1977; Harbach, 1994).

Wyeomyia aporonoma was originally described by Dyar and Knab in 1906. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the subgenus Triamyia, of which it is the type species (established by Edwards, 1932). Taxonomic stability has been maintained through major revisions of the Sabethini tribe, including the comprehensive catalogs by Knight and Stone (1977) and the subsequent updates in the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory. Morphological characteristics of the male genitalia and larval features distinguish it from other members of the genus Wyeomyia.

The species was originally described by Theobald (1903) based on specimens collected in Brazil. It is currently recognized as a valid and distinct species within the subgenus Sabethes. Its taxonomic status has remained stable, and it is frequently cited in Neotropical culicidology as a primary member of the sylvatic mosquito fauna in South America (Harbach, 2024).

The species was originally described by Dyar and Knab (1906) based on specimens from Santo Domingo. It is currently classified as a valid species within the subgenus Sabethes. The taxonomic status has remained stable throughout major Neotropical mosquito revisions, including the comprehensive work of Lane (1953) and current classifications maintained in the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory (Harbach, 2024).

The taxon was originally described as Verrallina leucocelaena by Dyar & Shannon (1924). It was later transferred to the genus Haemagogus. The name "conopostegus" mentioned in the query refers to the subgenus Conopostegus, established by Dyar (1928), to which this species belongs. According to the systematic revision by Arnell (1973) and the world catalog by Knight & Stone (1977), Haemagogus leucocelaenus is the valid specific name, while Conopostegus is its subgeneric classification. There is no valid subspecies or specific name "conopostegus leucocelaenus" as a trinomial; rather, it represents the subgenus and species combination.

Originalmente descrita como Culex fluviatilis por Lutz en 1904, la especie fue posteriormente transferida al género Aedes. Durante la reasignación taxonómica propuesta por Reinert et al. (2004), el subgénero Ochlerotatus fue elevado a nivel de género, clasificando a esta especie como Ochlerotatus fluviatilis. Sin embargo, siguiendo los criterios de Wilkerson et al. (2015), se ha restablecido la clasificación que considera a Ochlerotatus como un subgénero dentro de Aedes para mantener la estabilidad nomenclatural. Por lo tanto, el nombre aceptado actualmente bajo el consenso taxonómico mayoritario es Aedes fluviatilis.

The species was originally described by Neiva and Pinto in 1923. It is currently recognized as a valid species belonging to the subgenus Sabethoides. Taxonomic stability has been maintained through major revisions of the Sabethini tribe, including the classifications provided by Lane (1953) and subsequently confirmed in the catalogs of Knight and Stone (1977) and the Mosquito Taxonomic Inventory. The species is distinguished from others in the subgenus by specific morphological characters of the male genitalia and the patterns of metallic scales on the thorax and legs.

The taxon was originally described as a distinct species by Gordon and Evans (1922) based on specimens collected in Manaus, Brazil. Although the user referred to it as "Sabethes sabethes amazonicus," the correct systematic nomenclature identifies Sabethes as the genus and Sabethes as the subgenus, with amazonicus as the specific epithet. Current taxonomic classifications (Harbach, 2013; Knight & Stone, 1977) maintain Sabethes amazonicus as a valid species within the tribe Sabethini. There are no current subspecific divisions for this taxon.

The species was originally described by Theobald (1907) as Sabethes purpureus based on specimens collected in Brazil. It is currently recognized as a valid species within the subgenus Sabethes of the genus Sabethes. The taxonomic status has been maintained through various revisions of the tribe Sabethini, characterized by its metallic structural coloration and specific silver scales on the pleura. According to Harbach (2024), it remains a distinct biological entity within the Neotropical mosquito fauna.

Originally described as Janthinosoma albigenu by Peryassú (1908), this species is currently placed within the subgenus Janthinosoma of the genus Psorophora. Its taxonomic validity is supported by morphological distinctions in the adult female color patterns and male genitalic structures, which differentiate it from other members of the "Albipes" series. Lane (1953) corroborated its status in his comprehensive review of Neotropical Culicidae, separating it from Ps. albipes and Ps. varipes.

The species was originally described as Aedes hastatus by Dyar (1907). For a period following the taxonomic revision by Reinert (2000), which elevated the subgenus Ochlerotatus to the rank of genus, the name Ochlerotatus hastatus was widely used. However, a major reclassification of the tribe Aedini by Wilkerson et al. (2015) reverted Ochlerotatus to a subgeneric status within the genus Aedes to prioritize nomenclatural stability and reflect phylogenetic relationships. Under the current consensus utilized by the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit (WRBU) and the PINV01-528 project, the valid name is Aedes (Ochlerotatus) hastatus.

The species was originally described as Janthinosoma albipes by Theobald (1907). It was later reassigned to the genus Psorophora, subgenus Janthinosoma. It is a valid and distinct species, often differentiated from closely related species such as Psorophora ferox by the characteristic white scaling on the hindtarsomeres, specifically where hindtarsomeres 3, 4, and 5 are entirely white. Its taxonomic status as a full species is maintained in major mosquito catalogs (Knight & Stone, 1977; Harbach, 2024).

Originally described as Culex ferox by Humboldt (1819) from specimens collected in present-day Colombia. The species was later transferred to the genus Psorophora and placed within the subgenus Janthinosoma. It is recognized as a valid species and the type species for the Ferox Group. Its taxonomic status is supported by morphological characteristics of the adult female (conspicuous white scales on the hindtarsomeres) and male genitalia (Knight & Stone, 1977; Ward, 2005).

Limatus durhamii was described by Frederick Vincent Theobald in 1901 and serves as the type species for the genus Limatus. The taxonomic status of this species has remained stable as a valid taxon within the tribe Sabethini of the family Culicidae. It is widely distributed across the Neotropical region, from Mexico to Argentina (Theobald, 1901).

The species was originally described by Fabricius in 1794 under the name Culex ciliatus. It was later designated as the type species of the genus Psorophora by Robineau-Desvoidy in 1827. The current taxonomic classification places it within the subgenus Psorophora based on the morphological characteristics of the adult (large size, shaggy scales on legs) and larval stages, as detailed in the comprehensive revisions of the Culicidae (Knight & Stone, 1977; Belkin, 1962).
